cap1.abertura.p2: The war ended five years ago. The city still bears its scars, but the trams are running through the streets again, and in the parks the old men are back at their chessboards until dark.
cap1.abertura.p3: In the newspapers and on the radio, chess is serious business. The world champion is one of ours, Mikhail Botvinnik, and he has just been handed a challenger: the young master David Bronstein.
cap1.abertura.p4: You are thirteen. Your grandfather taught you the moves on a wooden board that still sits in your room.
cap1.abertura.p5: You don't know it yet, but this is where a road begins, one that could lead all the way to the throne.
cap1.quarto.livro.texto:
An old book of your grandfather's, its cover long gone, full of Capablanca's games. Grandfather used to say the Cuban played chess the way other people breathe: without any effort at all.

In the margins, his tiny handwriting insists, page after page: "Simplify. Always simplify."
cap1.quarto.tabuleiro.texto:
The wooden board where you learned the moves. The white knight has had a chipped ear ever since it fell off the table.

For weeks you have only played against yourself, turning the board around after every move. It is time to find real opponents.
cap1.fechamento.aprovado:
The sun has already set when Mr. Ozols puts the pieces back in their wooden box.

"You are not a beginner anymore," he says, without looking up from the box. "Tomorrow afternoon, wait for me here. I'll take you to a place where boys like you learn properly."
cap1.fechamento.reprovado:
Night falls over the park. The old men pack up their pieces and walk home arguing about the day's games.

Nobody is born knowing. Tomorrow they will be here again — and so will you.
adv.peteris.apresentacao: Eleven years old, pockets full of lost pieces. Plays fast and loves bringing his queen out early.
adv.grisha.apresentacao: A retired railwayman. Smokes a pipe, tells war stories and never turns down a queen trade.
adv.ozols.apresentacao: A watchmaker in his early sixties. The "king of the park": nobody remembers seeing him lose twice in a row.
dlg.peteris.inicio: Hey! Are you new here? I'm Pēteris. Old Ozols says I play too fast, but he's the one who plays too slow. Want a game? I'll take Black, it's my lucky colour.
dlg.peteris.depois_vitoria: Oh no! I was going to mate you next move… Almost. I'll get my revenge tomorrow, you'll see.
dlg.peteris.depois_derrota: See? Bringing the queen out early works! Tell Ozols, he never believes me.
dlg.peteris.depois_empate: A draw? Boring. Nobody wins anything with a draw.
dlg.grisha.inicio: Sit down, lad. Thirty years on the rails at Riga station, and now this is my train: sixty-four squares. I'll take White, if you don't mind. Old men have their habits.
dlg.grisha.guerra: During the war we played with pieces made of dried bread, on a board scratched into the lid of a box. When hunger got bad, a pawn that left the board didn't go back in the box… Well, enough sad stories. Shall we play?
dlg.grisha.depois_vitoria: Hmm. You calculate better than you look. A boy like you shouldn't stay in the park forever.
dlg.grisha.depois_derrota: Don't look so glum. I lost the first game of my life to my little brother, and he never let me forget it.
dlg.grisha.depois_empate: A fair draw. Like two engine drivers on the same track who both brake in time.
dlg.ozols.inicio: Hm. The new boy. I've heard about you. Here in the park I'm the last step, you understand? Whoever beats me can go and look for better opponents. Want to try?
dlg.ozols.depois_vitoria: … Well played. It's been a long time since anyone caught me like that. You need stronger people than this old man.
dlg.ozols.depois_derrota: Don't lose heart. I've been repairing watches for forty years: everything worth anything works with patience. Chess too.
dlg.ozols.depois_empate: A draw with old Ozols. That's not nothing, boy. That's not nothing.
dlg.marta.inicio: Good afternoon! Come to fetch your father's paper? Or are you here for the old chess players? They stay until dark.
dlg.marta.op_melhor: Who's the best in the park?
dlg.marta.novidades: It was in the paper: two of ours, Bronstein and Boleslavsky, tied for first in Budapest and had to play a whole match just to decide who challenges Botvinnik. Bronstein won. Soviet against Soviet for the chance to face another Soviet — imagine that!
dlg.marta.melhor: Mr. Ozols, the watchmaker. They say he once drew with a real master, but nobody saw it. He never denied it, either.
not.n1950_budapeste.titulo: A tie at the top in Budapest
not.n1950_budapeste.texto: The Candidates Tournament in Budapest ended with two Soviet players sharing first place: David Bronstein and Isaac Boleslavsky. One of them will be Mikhail Botvinnik's challenger.
not.n1950_desempate.texto: In the play-off match held in Moscow, David Bronstein beat Isaac Boleslavsky 7½–6½ — after the twelve scheduled games ended 6–6 — and won the right to play Mikhail Botvinnik for the world title.
not.n1950_titulos.texto: For the first time, the International Chess Federation has officially awarded the title of grandmaster, to 27 players. Eleven are Soviets — among them champion Botvinnik, Smyslov, Keres, Bronstein, Boleslavsky and the veteran Levenfish.
not.n1950_mezgailis.texto: Voldemārs Mežgailis has won the 1950 Latvian championship, repeating his title of 1944. The women's champion is Milda Lauberte.
not.n1950_final_urss.titulo: The Soviet championship final begins in Moscow
not.n1950_final_urss.texto: Eighteen masters are contesting the final of the 18th USSR Championship. Keres, Boleslavsky and Smyslov were seeded straight in; the rest came through the quarter-finals and semi-finals, including the one in Tartu, just over the border in Estonia.
dlg.marta.op_garoto: Are there any good boys here in Riga?
dlg.marta.garoto: There's Doctor Tal's son, Misha. He won the Latvian junior championship this year! They say that when he was even smaller he knocked on Botvinnik's door — the champion was on holiday here in Riga — asking for a game. The champion's wife told him he was asleep…
